title: Luke 21
description: Luke 21 in the Liberation and Inclusion Translation (LIT).
paragraphs: 1 When Jesusa looked up, he saw the rich depositing their gifts into the offering box. 2 He also saw an impoverished widow depositing two leptab there.

3 “Honestly, I’m telling you,” he said, “This widow who is experiencing poverty deposited more than all the others. 4 You see, the others deposited gifts from their excess, but she deposited from her lack everything she had to live on.”

5 While some were speaking about the sacred grounds, how it was adornedc with magnificent stones and offered items,d Jesuse said, 6 “As for these things you’re gazing at, the days will come when no stone will be left on another without being torn down.”
7 “Teacher,” they demanded, “Then when will these things happen? And what will be the sign when they’re coming?”

8 He said, “Watch that you aren’t led astray because many will come in my name, saying, ‘It’s me,’f and, ‘The time is near.’ Don’t follow them! 9 When you hear of battlesg and revolts,h don’t be terrified. You see, it’s necessary for these things to happen first, but that doesn’t mean the end is happening right away.”

10 Then he told them, “People groupi will be rousedj against people group and regimek will be roused against regime. 11 There will be violent earthquakes, famines, and plagues, and even terrors and dread signs from the heavens. 12 But before all these things, they will lay their hands onl you and persecute you, handing you over to the synagogues and prisons. You’ll be taken in front of kings and governors on account of my name.m 13 It will turn out as testimony for you.n 14 Therefore, settle it in your hearts not to rehearse a defense ahead of time.o 15 You see, I will give you a mouthp and wisdom which all the people set against you will not be able to oppose or contradict. 16 You will even be handed over by parents, siblings,q relatives, and friends, and they will put some of you to death. 17 You will be renouncedr by everyone on account of my name. 18 Yet not a single hair on your head will be lost.s 19 Wint your very selvesu with your endurance.

20 “But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, know that her ruinv has approached. 21 Then those in Judea must flee to the mountains. Those within Jerusalemw must evacuate, and those in the surrounding areas must not enter the cityx 22 because these are the days of reckoning,y of bringing aboutz everything that was written. 23 How heartbreakingaa for those who are pregnant and those who are nursing infants in those days! After all, it will be a huge disaster in the land and furybb against this people. 24 They will fall by the edgecc of the sword and be led away as captives among all peoples.dd Jerusalem will be trampled by other peoples, until the times appointed for other peoples are completed.

25 “There will be signs in the sun, moon, and stars,ee and on the earth, there will be a pressing-in upon the peoples, at a loss because of the roar and shaking of the sea; 26 there will be people fainting from fear and anticipation of what is coming upon the empire,ff for the powers of the heavensgg will be shaken. 27 Then they will see the Son of Humanityhh coming in a cloudii with power and immense honor.jj 28 When these things begin to happen, stand upright and hold your heads high because the purchase of your liberationkk is near!”

29 Then he told them a parable: “Look at the fig tree, and all the trees. 30 When they have sprouted leaves, you see for yourselves and know that summer is now near. 31 Similarly, when you see these things happening, know that God’s Reign is near. 32 Honestly, I’m telling you that this groupll will certainly not pass away until they all happen. 33 The heavens and the earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.

34 “Pay attention to yourselves, so that your hearts won’t be weighed downmm by hangover,nn drunkenness, and the stresses of daily life,oo and so that day won’t ambush you suddenly, 35 like a trap. After all, it will overtake everyone who lives on the face of the whole earth. 36 Be alert at every moment, praying, so that you would be strong enough to escape all these things that are going to happen and stand in the presence of the Son of Humanity.”

37 Each day Jesus was teaching in the sacred grounds, but each night he went and camped on the Mount of Olives. 38 And the entire people began rising at dawn to come listen to him in the sacred grounds.

footnotes.label: a
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: b
footnotes.html: A lepton was an extremely small copper coin, the least valuable in circulation, each worth about one one-hundred-twenty-eighth of a denarius, which was the standard day’s wage for a laborer. If we compare that to an eight-hour workday at a $15 wage, a single lepton would be worth just under one dollar.

footnotes.label: c
footnotes.html: Or ‘arranged’ or ‘ornamented’

footnotes.label: d
footnotes.html: The Greek word here translated as ‘offered items’ is anathema, the same word translated in Galatians 1:8 as ‘designated for destruction.’ The word broadly means something dedicated exclusively for God as an offering, which can be offered, at times, by destruction. In the Septuagint, anathema was used to translate the Hebrew word herem, traditionally translated ‘ban’ but has the same double meaning: something dedicated exclusively to God, whether positively as a gift or negatively as something to be destroyed. See ‘ban’ in Deuteronomy 7:1–2 and ‘reserved’ in Joshua 6:15–21.

footnotes.label: e
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: f
footnotes.html: Literally, “I am,” which was the standard Greek way to announce oneself.

footnotes.label: g
footnotes.html: Or ‘wars’

footnotes.label: h
footnotes.html: Or ‘uprisings’ or ‘upheavals’

footnotes.label: i
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘nations’ or ‘Gentiles.’ The word ethnoi literally means ‘nations’ (like ‘nationalities’ not ‘countries’) or ‘people groups’ and is where the English word ‘ethnicity’ comes from. It is usually—but not always—used in the Bible to refer to people groups other than the one the speaker belongs to, so typically to people groups other than Jews since most speakers/authors are Jewish.

footnotes.label: j
footnotes.html: The word egeiro has several uses, the most central being ‘get up’ or ‘wake up.’ It is one of the words referring to Jesus being raised from the dead, and it can mean literally standing up or waking up, as well as being presented as a public figure like a prophet.

footnotes.label: k
footnotes.html: The Greek word basileia can mean territories (“kingdoms”) or the governing systems that rule them (“kingship” or “reign”). Rendering it ‘regimes’ here (similarly to Luke 4:5) emphasizes that it is not about a piece of land but of the ruling powers striving against each other for even greater power.

footnotes.label: l
footnotes.html: This is referring to violently seizing or arresting someone, from as mild as forcefully restraining someone to as extreme as beating them severely in order to subdue them.

footnotes.label: m
footnotes.html: The phrase “because of my name” indicates that his reputation, what he is known for and stands for, is the basis or motivation for their actions.

footnotes.label: n
footnotes.html: This is an awkward sentence to translate directly, and very literally, it says “It will turn out/result to you as a testimony.” Most translations add some element of opportunity or time to give a testimony, but that’s not what it says. The idea is that the experiences described in verse 12 are themselves the testimony. There is no implication of action on the part of the audience.

footnotes.label: o
footnotes.html: It’s not just not rehearsing how to make a defense but not preparing to make a defense at all.

footnotes.label: p
footnotes.html: The word ‘mouth’ is translated from the Greek stoma. Many translations use ‘words,’ taking the obvious meaning but abandoning the larger idiom and imagery connecting to other threads. It was both a Hebraic and Greek idiom, not just for the body part that makes words or even the words themselves but as the ‘mouthpiece’ of something bigger. The Septuagint uses stoma in Exodus 4:11–12, 16, where it literally says, “Who gave a mouth to humanity?... I myself will be your mouth, and instruct you in what you are to say…. [Aaron] will be your mouth, and you will be to him what pertains to God” (that’s from the Greek; the Hebrew says “will be as God to him”). Then in Exodus 7:1, it states the idea again in different words: “I have made you a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother will be your prophet.” The imagery of ‘mouth’ isn’t just God providing a body part who speaks their own words; the image is of speaking someone else’s words, that someone else has spoken, and the one with the mouth is just the one the words come through. This also explains this passage’s instruction not to rehearse a defense. They’re not taking the role of defendant; they’re taking the role of prophet confronting the accusers with authority. The same word stoma, also paired with sophia (‘wisdom’), appears in Acts 6:10 when Stephen is accused and then does not defend himself but prophesies to his accusers.

footnotes.label: q
footnotes.html: The word adelphos literally means ‘brother’ or ‘sibling.’ It was also frequently used to refer to ‘cousin’ or ‘relative,’ and even for members of the same ideological or ethnic group.

footnotes.label: r
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘hated.’ The word ‘renounce’ renders the Greek miseo, which spans active postures of hostility and, in many Semitic contexts, the withdrawal or reversal of loyalty. It is not referring to an emotional state but a social posture that leads to actions taken against someone.

footnotes.label: s
footnotes.html: Or ‘be destroyed’ or ‘perish’ or ‘die’

footnotes.label: t
footnotes.html: The Greek word here (ktaomai) is different in various ancient manuscripts. The basic word is the same, but they vary as to whether they are future tense (describing something that will happen) or mandative (giving an instruction to do something). The SBLGNT text that this translation is based on sides with the mandative, which also seems to me to be the one that makes more sense in the context. Additionally, the traditional ‘gain’ is too passive for the meaning of this word. It is a much more active sense of acquiring, attaining, or winning something. It is not the same word translated as ‘gain’ in Luke 9:25 (kerdaino), despite the sentences being similar.

footnotes.label: u
footnotes.html: This is the word psuche, with the root idea of “breath.” It points to the breath, the respiration, that makes someone a living person. In the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, it is what is used to translate nephesh, or ‘living being.’ From there it takes on two closely linked meanings: 1, Physical life – When a verse is talking about someone’s body staying alive or being in danger, like “whoever wants to secure their psuche will surrender it” (Luke 9:24); 2, Inner self and identity – In many places psuche means the deep core of who you are, including your feelings, thoughts, priorities, values, motivation, and sense of self. That’s why Jesus asks, “how does it benefit a person to gain the whole world but injure or destroy their psuche?” (Luke 9:25). Here, the word is about more than staying alive; it’s about losing your identity and integrity of character. In these contexts it is translated as ‘very being’ or ‘very self.’ Psuche is the living person, seen from the angle of both survival and identity.

footnotes.label: v
footnotes.html: Or ‘being laid waste’ or ‘depopulation’

footnotes.label: w
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘her’

footnotes.label: x
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘her’

footnotes.label: y
footnotes.html: The Greek ekdikesis refers to the act of setting right a wrong, but the manner of setting it right varies based on context, who is taking action, and who is receiving the message. In Luke 18:7, the ones who cry out day and night receive ekdikesis from God, relief from their oppression. In Hosea 9:7, which Luke cites here, ekdikesis is the arrival of what the people, themselves being unjust, have set in motion.

footnotes.label: z
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘fulfill’

footnotes.label: aa
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘woe to’ or ‘alas for.’ The Greek word is ouai, and in modern English ‘woe’ sounds vague or archaic. It’s a prophetic outcry expressing both grief and warning. It’s not a curse but a lament for the harm people bring on themselves and each other through hypocrisy and injustice. Three renderings appear, based on who is in view: ‘how pitiful,’ where it is spoken toward people who are responsible for harm; ‘how pitiable,’ where it describes a condition and what is coming because of it; and ‘how heartbreaking,’ where grief is the only thing being expressed.

footnotes.label: bb
footnotes.html: The context is clearly about human fury, not divine fury, the fury of the invading armies of “other peoples” in the next verse.

footnotes.label: cc
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘mouth.’ This idiom comes originally from Hebrew, where the edge of the sword was called the mouth because it was thought of as devouring its victims. Compare this with the wordplay of a sword coming from Christ’s mouth instead of an emperor using the ‘mouth’ of a sword to acquire and maintain power in Revelation 19:15.

footnotes.label: dd
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘nations’ or ‘Gentiles.’ The word ethnoi literally means ‘nations’ (like ‘nationalities’ not ‘countries’) or ‘people groups’ and is where the English word ‘ethnicity’ comes from. It is usually—but not always—used in the Bible to refer to people groups other than the one the speaker belongs to, so typically to people groups other than Jews since most speakers/authors are Jewish.

footnotes.label: ee
footnotes.html: Compare with Isaiah 13:9–10, Ezekiel 32:7–8, and Joel 3:15

footnotes.label: ff
footnotes.html: The Greek term oikoumene is different than kosmos (‘world’). It refers specifically to “the known world” or “developed area” as opposed to the places inhabited by “uncivilized” (unconquered) peoples or vast, uninhabited wilderness. Essentially, it referred to the area controlled by the Roman Empire.

footnotes.label: gg
footnotes.html: ‘The heavens’ could refer to three ideas. The first is the literal meaning of ‘sky.’ The second is often assumed to be the meaning, the symbolic use to refer to wherever the divine presence is, the source of the Life-breath. The third is symbolic of social hierarchies, where Ouranos ‘the heavens’ referred to the powerful while ‘the earth’ referred to the common people. Sometimes, like in Paul’s letters, it’s divided even further from top to bottom as ‘highest heavens,’ ‘heavens,’ ‘air,’ ‘earth,’ and ‘below the earth,’ referring to the various socio-economic and power/status levels in the culture at the time.

footnotes.label: hh
footnotes.html: Reference to Ezekiel—“Son of Man” was how Ezekiel referred to himself—and to Daniel 7:13–27. This is one of the loftiest titles Jesus could have used for himself and likely played a key role in accusations against him of attempting to usurp the royal throne. At the same time, though Daniel 7:13–14 connects the “one like a son of humanity” to a kingship with all peoples serving him and that his kingship shall never be destroyed, continuing to verse 27 is the parallel verse that explains it further, and it asserts that “the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole heaven shall be given to the people” as an everlasting kingdom. It also left Jesus with deniability, since he could also claim just to be calling himself a prophet in the tradition of Ezekiel.

footnotes.label: ii
footnotes.html: Reference to Daniel 7:13–14

footnotes.label: jj
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘glory’

footnotes.label: kk
footnotes.html: What is translated here as “purchase of your liberation” is the word apolutrosis in Greek. It is traditionally translated as ‘ransom’ or ‘redemption.’ It literally means securing the release of someone from enslavement by paying the purchase price.

footnotes.label: ll
footnotes.html: Or ‘generation’ or ‘lineage’ or any ‘group of people’ that has a shared characteristic or origin, including gender.

footnotes.label: mm
footnotes.html: Compare with Luke 9:32, where the same word describes Peter and others being weighed down by sleep and not being ready to respond.

footnotes.label: nn
footnotes.html: The word ‘hangover’ is translating the Greek word kraipale, which overwhelmingly referred to the aftermath of heavy drinking. While some uses of the related verb form in the Septuagint (Isaiah 24:20; 29:9) referred to the heavy drinking itself, the noun consistently applies to the hangover afterward.

footnotes.label: oo
footnotes.html: The Greek word translated here as ‘of daily life’ is the adjective biotikos, describing the ‘stresses’ as ones having to do with practical life, how it’s lived and sustained. The word biotikos is the adjective form of the noun bios, which appears earlier in this chapter, in verse 4, where the widow deposits ‘all the bios she had’ or ‘everything she had to live on.’
